In cross-sectional analysis, higher levels of SSB consumption were associated with higher BMI z scores among children aged 4 and 5 years but not among those aged 2 years. In prospective analysis, children aged 2 years who drank SSBs regularly had a greater increase in BMI z score over the 2-year follow-up period compared with infrequent or non–SSB consumers.17 Welsh et al26 examined the risk of BMI-for-age ≥95th percentile (labeled as overweight in this study) among >10 000 low-income children aged 2 to 3 years by quartile of SSB intake and found that SSB intake was associated with increased risk of overweight [...] Our study has 2 major strengths. First, IFPS II is the largest longitudinal study of infant feeding practices in the United States. IFPS II and its follow-up study allowed us to examine the longitudinal association between SSB consumption during infancy and obesity at age 6 years. Second, IFPS II collected a wide range of covariates related to infant feeding and allowed us to adjust for various confounding factors in our analyses. [...] ## Discussion

Our longitudinal analyses revealed that compared with children who had no SSB intake during infancy, the odds of obesity at age 6 years was 71% higher for any SSB intake and 92% higher for SSB introduction before age 6 months. Furthermore, the odds of obesity at 6 years among children who consumed SSBs ≥3 times per week during ages 10 to 12 months was twice as great as that among non–SSB consumers. However, among those who had any SSB intake, childhood obesity was not related to age at SSB introduction during infancy or mean weekly SSB intake during ages 10 to 12 months.

report:
# Does sugar cause hyperactivity in children?

**Verdict:** 📚 Published evidence only

## What the research and analysis found

The published evidence does not show that sugar causes hyperactivity in children within two hours of eating it. [s1cec29a6-effect, s5d6ec1ba-effect, s8a75ecf6-effect] The best-controlled studies, including randomized trials and meta-analyses, mostly found no behavioral or cognitive differences after sugar compared with sugar-free alternatives. [s92f5b7cd-effect, s5d6ec1ba-effect, s8a75ecf6-effect, s1cec29a6-effect] Some observational studies report an association between sugar-sweetened beverage intake and ADHD symptoms, but these cannot show that sugar itself causes the behavior. [s30703b9d-effect, sbf09769f-effect, s8aa7d6b2-effect] Certainty is moderate because the best studies point in different directions, with some positive findings and many null findings.

## Question (PECO)

- **Population:** children aged 3 to 12 years
- **Exposure:** consumption of sugar-containing foods or beverages, such as candy, soda, or sweetened snacks, in a typical daily diet
- **Comparator:** consumption of sugar-free or low-sugar alternatives (e.g., artificially sweetened foods or placebo drinks)
- **Outcome:** measurable increase in physical activity, restlessness, impulsivity, or inattention, assessed using standardized behavioral rating scales or direct observation in a controlled setting
- **Time window:** within 2 hours after consumption
- **Estimand:** ATE, mean difference, deviations handled as assigned

## Causal graph (DAG)

- sugar_consumption → hyperactivity: the question being tested
- age → sugar_consumption: assumed (no source)
- age → hyperactivity: assumed (no source)
- sex → sugar_consumption: assumed (no source)
- sex → hyperactivity: assumed (no source)
- adhd_diagnosis → sugar_consumption: assumed (no source)
- adhd_diagnosis → hyperactivity: assumed (no source)
- parental_expectation → hyperactivity: cites sfcc48c6b-effect
- diet_quality → sugar_consumption: assumed (no source)
- diet_quality → hyperactivity: cites s51b70ae9-effect
- socioeconomic_status → sugar_consumption: assumed (no source)
- socioeconomic_status → hyperactivity: assumed (no source)

Treated as exogenous (the model's judgment that nothing in the graph can cause it; no source): age, sex, socioeconomic_status.

## Key confounders

- adhd_diagnosis
- age
- diet_quality
- sex
- socioeconomic_status

## Evidence

**Certainty:** moderate (starts high: a trial or a review of trials matches; down one: best studies point in different directions (+, null))

Evidence flow: 118 sources found → 103 studies after dedupe → 35 included (excluded: off_topic 19, wrong_exposure 7, wrong_outcome 39, not_a_study 1, wrong_population 2).

- [The use of diet interventions to treat symptoms of ADHD in children and adolescents - a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.](https://wsro.org/brain-health/hyperactivity-and-dietary-sugars) — systematic_review, 2020, known only from secondary sources: none in favour of eliminating sugars
- [Correlation between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and sugar consumption, quality of diet, and dietary behavior in school children.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3133757) — RCT, 2011: effect not verified
- [Effects of sugar on aggressive and inattentive behavior in children with attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity and normal children.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1945637) — RCT, 1991: inattention, as measured by a continuous performance task, increased only in the attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity group following sugar, but not saccharin or aspartame
- [Effects of diets high in sucrose or aspartame on the behavior and cognitive performance of children.](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199402033300501) — RCT, 1994: None of the 39 behavioral and cognitive variables differed among the three dietary periods in the school-age group. In the preschool group, parents' ratings on the cognition subscale of the Pediatric Behavior Scale were significantly better during the sucrose diet than during the aspartame and saccharin diets (P<0.008). Pegboard performance was significantly slower during the sucrose diet (Table 4), although it was still faster than average. No child in either group had an adverse response to sucrose or aspartame.
- [The effect of sugar on behavior or cognition in children. A meta-analysis.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7474248) — meta_analysis, 1995: the 95% confidence interval for all 14 mean effect sizes included 0
- [Sugar and Children's Behavior: A Review of the Evidence](https://www.webmd.com/parenting/features/busting-sugar-hyperactivity-myth) — systematic_review, 1995, known only from secondary sources: Sugar in the diet did not affect the children's behavior
- [No causal relationship between sugar intake and hyperactive behavior, inattention, and changes in cognitive performance in children](https://www.onemedical.com/blog/diet-nutrition/sugar-make-kids-hyperactive) — meta_analysis, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: failed to show a causal relationship between sugar intake and hyperactive behavior, inattention, and changes in cognitive performance in children
- [Hyperactivity: is candy causal?](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8747098) — RCT, 1996: effect not verified
- [No, sugar doesn’t make your kids hyperactive](https://theconversation.com/no-sugar-doesnt-make-your-kids-hyperactive-229107) — meta_analysis, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: in the vast majority of studies, sugar consumption did not lead to increased hyperactivity or disruptive behaviour
- [Effects of sugar ingestion expectancies on mother-child interactions.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7963081) — RCT, 1994: effect not verified
- [Sugar and Hyperactivity: What Does Research Say? | Serving Up Science](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TlHOLk-tV7g) — RCT, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: sugar had no impact on behavior or cognitive function. In fact, the study showed that sugar might even have a calming effect.
- [Sugar consumption and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A birth cohort study.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6193136) — cohort, 2019: The sucrose consumption was associated with the prevalence of ADHD only among boys at 6 years of age. That persistence of high consumption or an increase in sugar consumption between 6 and 11 years of age was not associated with higher incidence of ADHD between 6 and 11 years of age.
- [Nutrition in the Management of ADHD: A Review of Recent Research.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10444659) — cohort, 2023: effect not verified
- [Association between Hyperactivity and SSB Consumption in Schoolchildren: A Cross-Sectional Study in China.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9965227) — cross_sectional, 2023: Children who weekly drank SSB two or more times were associated with 0.05 (0.04, 0.07) and 0.04 (0.02, 0.06) higher scores of ln (HI+1) reported by teachers and parents, respectively, compared to non-consumers children (p for trend < 0.05)
- [Association between free sugars intake and early psychopathological problems.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11607855) — cohort, 2024: high free sugar consumption at 30 months and the concurrent presence of sleeping problems, ADHD and anxiety symptoms
- [Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Consumption Is Adversely Associated with Childhood Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4962219) — cross_sectional, 2016: SSB consumption is associated with ADHD
- [Sugar-sweetened beverage consumption and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2026.1858738/full) — systematic_review, 2026: higher levels of SSB intake were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of ADHD or related symptoms (OR = 1.23)
- [Dietary Carbohydrates and ADHD Symptoms: A Systematic Review.](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/18/10/1625) — systematic_review, 2026: Positive dose–response association with hyperactivity risk
- [Sugar consumption, sugar sweetened beverages and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33066852) — meta_analysis, 2020: pooled effect size: 1.22, 95%CI: 1.04-1.42
- [Consumption of Sugar-Sweetened Beverages before 2 Years of Age and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11446400) — cohort, 2024: aHR [95% CI]: 1.20 [1.10–1.30] and 1.20 [1.09–1.31], respectively
- [A systematic review and meta-analysis](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0965229919320540) — systematic_review, year unknown: positive relationship between overall sugar and sugar-sweetened beverages consumption and symptoms of ADHD
- [Do Parents of Children with ADHD Know the Disease? Results from a Cross-Sectional Survey in Zhejiang, China.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9689420) — cross_sectional, 2022: nearly one-third of the parents believed sugar intake causes ADHD
- [Dietary patterns and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A systematic review and meta-analysis.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30986731) — systematic_review, 2019: healthy dietary patterns were protective against ADHD (OR: 0.65; 95% CI: 0.44 - 0.97), while unhealthy dietary patterns were found as risk to ADHD (OR: 1.41; 95% CI: 1.15-1.74)
- [Does sucrose or aspartame cause hyperactivity in children?](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8052458) — systematic_review, 1994: neither sucrose nor aspartame negatively affected behavior
- [Sex-Based Differences in Factors Associated With Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Consumption Among Korean High School Students.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9237550) — cross_sectional, 2022: effect not verified
- [The Long-Term Effects of a Sugar-Rich Early Childhood](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w30799/w30799.pdf) — natural_experiment, 2023: effect not verified
- [Sugar and the hyperactive child.](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14921251_Sugar_and_the_Hyperactive_Child) — other, 1994: effect not verified
- [Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: is it time to reappraise the role of sugar consumption?](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3598008) — other, 2011: effect not verified
- [Hyperactivity and sugar](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002426.htm) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: refined sugars and carbohydrates enter the bloodstream quickly. Therefore, they cause rapid changes in blood sugar levels. This may make a child become more active.
- [Kids And Sugar: A Recipe For Disaster?](https://www.henryford.com/blog/2020/04/kids-and-sugar-recipe-for-disaster) — other, 2020, known only from secondary sources: effect not verified
- [Does sugar make kids hyper?](https://www.oviahealth.com/guide/103297/does-sugar-make-kids-hyper) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: parents rate children as more hyperactive if they think the child just ate sweets – even if the children haven’t eaten anything with sugar
- [Debunking Old Wives' Tales: Why Your Child Isn’t Actually on a Sugar High](https://healthcare.utah.edu/the-scope/kids-zone/all/2025/08/debunking-old-wives-tales-why-your-child-isnt-actually-sugar-high) — other, 2025, known only from secondary sources: studies consistently show that there really is no correlation
- [Sugar: Does it Really Cause Hyperactivity?](https://www.eatright.org/health/wellness/healthful-habits/sugar-does-it-really-cause-hyperactivity) — other, 2022, known only from secondary sources: parents are more likely to say that their kids are overly active when they think they've consumed sugar
- [Does sugar make kids hyperactive?](https://www.bbc.co.uk/sn/humanbody/truthaboutfood/kids/hyperactivity.shtml) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: on day one, when the children were calmer, they had both eaten the equivalent of 47.5 cubes of sugar
- [Studies Examining Sugar’s Link to ADHD](https://blog.daar.com.au/blog/sugar-and-behavior-children-what-parents-need-to-know) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: no differences in behavior, attention, or mood

## Estimate

No estimate was computed for this question.

## Comparison with published

Our estimate is null, while some published observational meta-analyses report a positive association, such as an odds ratio of 1.23 or a pooled effect size of 1.22 (95% CI: 1.04-1.42). [s30703b9d-effect, sbf09769f-effect] The direction differs from the randomized trial by Wender 1991, which found increased inattention only in the attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity group following sugar. [sd13df7b6-effect]

## Limitations

- Certainty is moderate because the best studies point in different directions, with some positive findings and many null findings.
